BGG.com is the premier source for information on boardgames, but its interface is archaic even to those who know how to use it. Enter /r/boardgames which has a larger potential user base because of the reddit.com population.

From what I've observed, one of the best ways to get a game noticed is to get it at the top of the Hotness list of BGG which is (likely) based on pageviews for a game. A direct link from /r/boardgames submitted at a specific time has the potential to reach thousands of visitors. It was pretty apparent this happened when an out of print game from the 80s shot up to the top of the hotness after a nostalgic title with a direct link made it to the top post. Unfortunately I can't remember the game or the post that caused this incident.

Success for a game could come with a clever title and a timely posting, and the potential viewers of this one link could cause a ripple effect, creating more and more pageviews as frequenters of BGG check out an unknown title at the top of the hotness.
Power balance between /r/boardgames and BGG.com and the best way to get a game noticed

This happened a few days ago with the Rodney Dangerfield game. Topped the hotness because of a prank at BGG.fam or some such.

Yes, there is definitely a way to game the system. /r/circlejerk frequently makes fun of posts using autism, cats, girls/boobs/etc, and for good reason.

There's probably a karma-whore equivalent in the boardgames world, but I haven't found it!
